extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, safety/hazard classification personnel, and regulatory compliance officers responsible for classifying chemicals and preparing labels and safety data sheets under OSHA/GHS
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory criteria and labeling requirements for classifying physical hazards of chemicals (self-reactive chemicals, pyrophorics, oxidizers, organic peroxides, desensitized explosives, corrosives to metals, etc.) and for allocating label elements (signal words, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, supplementary information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reactive chemical types A–G
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions/classification of self-reactive chemicals into Types A through G based on whether, as packaged or in laboratory testing, they detonate, deflagrate rapidly, undergo thermal explosion, show violent/medium/low/no effect when heated under confinement, and whether they detonate in the cavitated state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type A: can detonate or deflagrate rapidly as packaged. Type B: possess explosive properties, do not detonate/deflagrate rapidly as packaged but liable to undergo thermal explosion in that package. Type C: possess explosive properties when packaged but cannot detonate/deflagrate rapidly or undergo thermal explosion. Type D: lab testing meets (i) detonates partially, does not deflagrate rapidly and shows no violent effect when heated under confinement; or (ii) does not detonate, deflagrates slowly and shows no violent effect; or (iii) does not detonate or deflagrate and shows a medium effect when heated under confinement. Type E: neither detonates nor deflagrates and shows low or no effect when heated under confinement. Type F: neither detonates in cavitated state nor deflagrates and shows low/no effect when heated under confinement and low/no explosive power. Type G: neither detonates in cavitated state nor deflagrates, shows no effect when heated under confinement nor any explosive power, provided it is thermally stable (SADT 60 °C–75 °C for 50 kg package) and for liquid mixtures a diluent boiling point ≥150 °C is used; otherwise classify as Type F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reactive chemicals — additional classification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties of self-reactive chemicals must be determined in accordance with UN ST/SG/AC.10 test series A–H; SADT shall be determined per Part II, section 28 of UN ST/SG/AC.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification procedures need not be applied if (a) no chemical groups associated with explosive or self-reactive properties are present (examples in UN ST/SG/AC.10 Appendix 6 Tables A6.1/A6.2), or (b) for single organic substances or homogeneous organic mixtures estimated SADT >75 °C or exothermic decomposition energy <300 J/g (onset temperature and decomposition energy may be estimated using suitable calorimetric technique per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part II §20.3.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrophoric liquid — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyrophoric liquid: a liquid which, even in small quantities, is liable to ignite within five minutes after coming into contact with air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify using test N.3 (Part III, sub-section 33.3.1.5 UN ST/SG/AC.10) and Table B.9.1: Category 1 if liquid ignites within 5 minutes when added to an inert carrier and exposed to air, or ignites/char a filter paper on contact with air within 5 minutes. Classification need not be applied when production/handling experience shows the chemical does not ignite spontaneously at normal temperatures (stable at room temperature for prolonged periods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrophoric solid — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyrophoric solid: a solid which, even in small quantities, is liable to ignite within five minutes after coming into contact with air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify using test N.2 (Part III, sub-section 33.3.1.4 UN ST/SG/AC.10) and Table B.10.1: Category 1 if the solid ignites within 5 minutes of coming into contact with air. Classification of solids is based on tests performed on the chemical as presented; if supplied/presented in a different physical form likely to alter performance, classification must be based on testing of the new form. Procedure need not be applied when handling experience shows stability at room temperature for prolonged periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-heating chemicals — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-heating chemical: a solid or liquid (other than pyrophoric) that, by reaction with air and without external energy, is liable to self-heat and may ignite only when in large amounts and after long periods (hours/days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify per test N.4 (Part III, sub-section 33.3.1.6 UN ST/SG/AC.10) using Table B.11.1: Category 1 if positive with 25 mm cube at 140 °C; Category 2 if negative with 25 mm at 140 °C but positive with 100 mm at 140 °C and unit volume >3 m3, or positive with 100 mm at 120 °C and unit volume >450 L, or positive with 100 mm at 100 °C. Chemicals with spontaneous combustion temperature >50 °C for 27 m3 (or >50 °C for 450 L w.r.t Category 1) shall not be classified as self-heating (or in Category 1 respectively). Classification procedure need not be applied if a screening test correlates adequately with the classification test with an appropriate safety margin; example screening tests: Grewer Oven (onset temp 80 K above ref temp for 1 L) and Bulk Powder Screening Test (onset temp 60 K above ref temp for 1 L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemicals which in contact with water emit flammable gases — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemicals which, in contact with water, emit flammable gases: solids or liquids which, by interaction with water, are liable to become spontaneously flammable or give off flammable gases in dangerous quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify using test N.5 (Part III, sub-section 33.4.1.4 UN ST/SG/AC.10) and Table B.12.1: Category criteria are based on behavior of 1:1 mass mixtures of chemical and cellulose comparing spontaneous ignition or mean pressure rise time against reference mixtures (50% perchloric acid, 40% sodium chlorate, 65% nitric acid). A chemical is classified if spontaneous ignition occurs in any test step. Classification need not be applied if (a) chemical structure contains no metals/metalloids, (b) production/handling experience shows it does not react with water, or (c) chemical is known to be soluble in water forming a stable mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxidizing liquids — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxidizing liquid: a liquid which, while not necessarily combustible itself, may by yielding oxygen cause or contribute to combustion of other material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify using test O.2 (Part III, sub-section 34.4.2 UN ST/SG/AC.10) and Table B.13.1: Category criteria mirror those in B.12 (1:1 mixture with cellulose; spontaneous ignition or mean pressure rise time compared to reference perchloric/sodium chlorate/nitric acid mixtures). Do not apply procedure for organic chemicals if they do not contain oxygen/fluorine/chlorine or if those elements are bonded only to carbon or hydrogen; for inorganic chemicals do not apply if no oxygen or halogen atoms. If test results diverge from known handling experience, known experience takes precedence. If pressure rise is caused by non-oxidizing reactions, repeat test substituting an inert substance (e.g., diatomite) for cellulose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxidizing solids — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxidizing solid: a solid which, while not necessarily combustible, may by yielding oxygen cause or contribute to combustion of other material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify using test O.1 (Part III, sub-section 34.4.1) or test O.3 (Part III, sub-section 34.4.3 UN ST/SG/AC.10/11) and Table B.14.1: Categories based on mean burning time (O.1) or mean burning rate (O.3) in sample-to-cellulose ratios compared to reference mixtures (potassium bromate/cellulose and calcium peroxide/cellulose). Notes: some oxidizing solids may present explosion hazards under certain conditions (e.g., ammonium nitrate) and additional tests (Resistance to detonation) may be used. Classification based on tests of chemical as presented; re-test when physical form changes. Additional considerations parallel oxidizing liquids: organic/inorganic compositional exemptions and precedence of handling experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic peroxides — definition and classification (Types A–G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic peroxide: an organic chemical containing the bivalent -O-O- structure (derivative of hydrogen peroxide) including mixtures containing at least one organic peroxide. They are thermally unstable and may be liable to explosive decomposition, burn rapidly, be sensitive to impact/friction, or react dangerously with other substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An organic peroxide is regarded as possessing explosive properties when lab testing shows it is liable to detonate, deflagrate rapidly, or show violent effect when heated under confinement. Consider for classification unless it contains ≤1.0% available oxygen when ≤1.0% hydrogen peroxide, or ≤0.5% available oxygen when >1.0%–7.0% hydrogen peroxide (available oxygen computed by formula provided). Classify into Types A–G: Type A (can detonate or deflagrate rapidly as packaged); Type B (possess explosive properties, do not detonate/deflagrate rapidly as packaged but liable to thermal explosion); Type C (possess explosive properties but as packaged cannot detonate/deflagrate rapidly or undergo thermal explosion); Type D (laboratory criteria as per D(i)-(iii) analogous to self-reactive D); Type E (neither detonates/deflagrates and shows low/no effect when heated); Type F (neither detonates in cavitated state nor deflagrates and low/no effect and low/no explosive power); Type G (neither detonates in cavitated state nor deflagrates and shows no effect or explosive power provided thermally stable — SADT ≥60 °C for a 50 kg package — and for liquid mixtures diluent boiling point ≥150 °C; otherwise classify as Type F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic peroxides — additional classification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties determined using UN ST/SG/AC.10 test series A–H; SADT determined per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part II section 28; mixtures may be classified as the same type as the most dangerous ingredient but SADT of mixture must be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixtures of stable ingredients can form thermally less stable mixtures; therefore determine SADT of the mixture. Testing methods references and SADT thresholds mirror self-reactive chemicals guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrosive to metals — definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical corrosive to metals: a chemical which by chemical action will materially damage or destroy metals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify in single category using test in Part III, sub-section 37.4 UN ST/SG/AC.10 and Table B.16.1: Category 1 if corrosion rate on either steel or aluminum surfaces exceeds 6.25 mm per year at test temperature 55 °C when tested on both materials. If initial test indicates corrosive on either steel or aluminum, follow-up test on the other metal not necessary. Specimen materials for testing are specified (steel types S235JR+CR, S275J2G3+CR, ISO 3574, UNS G10200, SAE 1020; aluminium non-clad types 7075-T6 or AZ5GU-T6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitized explosives — definitions and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Desensitized explosives: solid or liquid explosive chemicals phlegmatized (wetted, diluted or dissolved) to suppress explosive properties so they do not mass explode or burn too rapidly and may be exempted from hazard class Explosives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class comprises (a) solid desensitized explosives (wetted with water/alcohols or diluted to form homogeneous solid mixture; includes desensitization by hydrate formation) and (b) liquid desensitized explosives (dissolved or suspended in water or other liquids to form homogeneous liquid mixture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitized explosives — classification criteria and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any desensitized explosive for this class unless it is intended to produce a practical explosive/pyrotechnic effect, has a mass explosion hazard according to test series 6(a) or 6(b) or corrected burning rate >1200 kg/min, or its exothermic decomposition energy is <300 J/g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify into four categories based on corrected burning rate (Ac) using the 'burning rate test (external fire)' (Part V, sub-section 51.4 UN ST/SG/AC.10/11/Rev.6): Category 1: Ac ≥300 kg/min and ≤1200 kg/min; Category 2: 140 ≤ Ac < 300 kg/min; Category 3: 60 ≤ Ac < 140 kg/min; Category 4: Ac < 60 kg/min. Notes: desensitized explosives must remain homogeneous and not separate during normal storage/handling; manufacturer/importer/distributor must provide SDS Section 10 info on shelf-life and instructions for verifying desensitization; Sections 5 and/or 8 of SDS should advise on avoiding increased hazards when chemical is not sufficiently desensitized. Explosive properties shall be determined using data from Test Series 2; testing of liquid and solid desensitized explosives referenced to specific sections of UN ST/SG/AC.10/11/Rev.6. Desensitized explosives do not additionally fall within chapters B.1, B.6, B.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitized explosives — additional classification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure does not apply if substances/mixtures contain no explosives per Chapter B.1 or exothermic decomposition energy is <300 J/g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exothermic decomposition energy shall be determined using the explosive already desensitized (the homogeneous mixture) and may be estimated using suitable calorimetric technique (see referenced UN ST/SG/AC.10/11/Rev.6 guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Label product identifier and contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: The label for each hazardous chemical shall include the product identifier used on the safety data sheet; labels on shipped containers shall also include the name, address, and telephone number of the chemical manufacturer, importer, or responsible party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mandatory label elements (Appendix C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory label elements — signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The label for each classified hazardous chemical shall include the signal word, hazard statement(s), pictogram(s), and precautionary statement(s) specified in C.4 for each hazard class and associated hazard category, except as provided in specified exceptions (C.2.1–C.2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All applicable standardized elements must be present unless specific exceptions allow omission or modification under rules provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence rules for hazard information on labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules specifying precedence when multiple label elements could conflict or duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the signal word 'Danger' is included, 'Warning' shall not appear. If the skull-and-crossbones pictogram is included, the exclamation mark pictogram shall not appear where used for acute toxicity. If the corrosive pictogram is included, exclamation mark shall not appear where used for skin/eye irritation. If health hazard pictogram is included for respiratory sensitization, the exclamation mark shall not appear where used for skin sensitization or skin/eye irritation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard statement text — requirements and combining
rubrics_metrics.description: Text of all applicable hazard statements shall appear on the label, including italicized parts as part of the hazard statement; statements may be combined to reduce label content so long as all hazards are conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format: 'causes damage to organs (state all organs affected) through prolonged or repeated exposure (state route of exposure if no other routes cause the hazard)'. A manufacturer/importer/responsible party may demonstrate that parts of a hazard statement are inappropriate for a specific substance/mixture and omit the corresponding statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictograms — design and permitted use
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictograms must be square set at a point, include a black hazard symbol on white background with a red frame sufficiently wide to be clearly visible; a red frame without a hazard symbol is not a pictogram and is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of eight standard hazard symbols shall be used in each pictogram (depicted in Figure C.1). The exclamation mark pictogram is permitted (but not required) for HNOCs if the words 'Hazard Not Otherwise Classified' or 'HNOC' appear below the pictogram. Pictograms may only appear once on a label; if multiple hazards require same pictogram it may not be repeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautionary statements — types and text rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of precautionary statements: 'prevention', 'response', 'storage', and 'disposal'. The core part of the precautionary statement is presented in bold and is the text that shall appear on the label except as otherwise specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a slash (/) appears it indicates a choice between phrases (the supplier selects the most appropriate). Ellipses ('...') indicate not all applicable conditions are listed (supplier to specify other conditions). Italic text indicates explanatory/conditional notes not intended to appear on the label. Square brackets [ ] indicate optional text to be used only under specified conditions; conditions for use explain when bracketed text should be used (e.g., if ventilation info is provided at point of use). Precautionary statements may be combined/consolidated to save space and improve readability. Minor textual variations (spelling, synonyms) are permitted if they assist communication and do not dilute safety information; must be used consistently on label and SDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautionary statements — prioritization and medical response rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for selecting and prioritizing precautionary/medical response statements when multiple hazards trigger similar statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple different precautionary statements are triggered, apply a prioritization system. If the same medical response statement is triggered multiple times, include only one statement reflecting the highest level of urgency, combined with at least one route of exposure or symptom 'IF' statement. Routes of exposure may be combined when triggered with a medical response statement — if triggered with three or more routes, 'IF exposed or concerned' may be used, but relevant 'IF' statements describing symptoms must be included in full. If a route is triggered multiple times it need only be included once. Exceptions: 'Get medical advice/attention if you feel unwell' or 'Get immediate medical advice/attention' combined with an 'If' statement must appear without prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary hazard information — limits and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary (non-standardized) information on the label is limited to cases where it provides further detail and does not contradict or cast doubt on standardized hazard information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement of supplemental information shall not impede identification of required information. Where an ingredient with unknown acute toxicity is used at ≥1% and the mixture is not classified based on testing of the mixture as a whole, the label and SDS are required to state that X% of the mixture consists of ingredient(s) of unknown acute toxicity (oral/dermal/inhalation).
